verdicts.evidence: GAO blog, 31 July 2024: "these institutions are generally not required to reimburse victims who have authorized payments as a result of a scam."

PwC: "PSPs must reimburse consumers who have fallen victim to an APP scam when using Faster Payments"; "split 50:50 between sending and receiving PSPs"; payments "on or after 7 October 2024". 'Most' holds on outcomes: PSR says 65% of all claims and 97% of in-scope claims are reimbursed. No source note sits beside this claim on the page.

Judged on the REPORTED sentence in the tagged passage (the review finding). PSR: "APP fraud losses have fallen by an estimated £73 million per year"; "Reimbursement rates for all claims have risen from 54% to 65%"; evaluator Frontier Economics, called an independent review.

Labeled inference, but stated as a general rule from one evaluated case. The source is a first-year evaluation of one UK policy; Frontier says it met "short-term objectives" and that "longer-term impacts on competition, innovation and market behaviour remain uncertain". The page's own WATCH list says how much of the drop would have happened anyway is open. The review reports lower losses and fewer scams; it does not establish a general law.
verdicts.fix: In Britain, after the banks were made to pay, losses fell. That suggests a bank that pays for the harm has a reason to build the second alarm.

verdicts.evidence: Detroit Free Press/Spokesman-Review, 3 Apr 2026, on FTC testimony of 25 Mar 2026: impostor scams drew more than 1 million reports and more than $3.5 billion in reported losses.

Labeled inference. Atlanta Fed quotes Reg E: unauthorized transfer is one "initiated by a person other than the consumer without authority"; institutions argue consumer-initiated transfers are not 'unauthorized'. GAO: authorized-scam victims generally not owed reimbursement. The page notes the exceptions (Zelle refunds) elsewhere.

12 CFR 1005.6(b)(1): liability "shall not exceed the lesser of $50" with notice "within two business days after learning of the loss or theft of the access device"; (b)(2): otherwise "shall not exceed the lesser of $500". 'Generally' covers the 60-day statement rule in (b)(3). Note: the clock runs from learning of the loss, and the Atlanta Fed post does not mention the $50/$500 limits at all; only the CFR supports this.

GAO: a "bank, credit union, or a payment app" ... "are generally not required to reimburse victims who have authorized payments as a result of a scam." Atlanta Fed supports only the preceding sentence (institutions argue such transfers are not 'unauthorized').

Reuters via The Star, 13 Nov 2023: banks on Zelle "began reversing transfers as of June 30" for imposter scams by fraudsters posing as "a government agency, bank or existing service provider"; Early Warning Services calls it "well above existing legal and regulatory requirements".

PSR, 1 July 2026: "There is no evidence of market exits or reckless consumer behaviour"; "outcomes can still vary to some degree depending on who consumers bank with". The stat block above the tag also checks out: 54% to 65% of all claims; 97% of in-scope claims; £73m per year; "nearly 35,000" fewer scams "due to the policy".

Judged on the stat block this tag closes. Spokesman-Review: $15.9 billion in 2025, a record, up from $12.5 billion; bank payments led payment methods by losses, followed by cryptocurrency; FTC testimony to the Joint Economic Committee, 25 March 2026. The $870M figure in the same block is not FTC data; it is the CFPB allegation and is worded 'alleged' (see c012).

Engadget: CFPB filed in December against Early Warning Services, JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America and Wells Fargo; per the CFPB, customers of the three banks "had lost more than $870 million during the seven years Zelle has been active". NPR: suit brought at the end of December; dropped Tuesday (4 March 2025). The ALLEGED tag fits the $870M figure; the filing and the dismissal are matters of record.
Zelle spokesperson: the lawsuit was "without merit, and legally and factually flawed" (Engadget update 5 Mar 2025; same words in NPR).

Labeled inference; rests on Monzo being a bank, not a gambling operator (Finextra release describes the block as a Monzo banking feature). No source on Monzo's revenue was read; the claim does not need one.

Open question still open as far as could be checked: a web search for U.S. bank self-serve gambling blocks returned only U.K., Irish and Australian banks. One search only; absence of results is not proof none exists.

15 U.S.C. 1643(a)(1)(B): "the liability is not in excess of $50"; 1643(b): "the burden of proof is upon the card issuer to show that the use was authorized"; credit line: "as added Pub. L. 91-508, title V, §502(a), Oct. 26, 1970".

15 U.S.C. 1693g(a): "$50"; "may not exceed a total of $500"; "within two business days after the consumer learns of the loss or theft"; added by Pub. L. 95-630, Nov. 10, 1978. Reg E 1005.6 carries the same limits. No source note sits beside this claim and 1693g is not in the page's source list.
Reuters via The Star: banks "began reversing transfers as of June 30" (2023); change made "to address consumer protection concerns raised by U.S. lawmakers and the federal consumer watchdog".

Regulation Tomorrow on PS24/7: maximum "£85,000 per claim", which "had previously been set at £415,000"; start 7 October 2024. PwC: "split 50:50 between sending and receiving PSPs"; claims "not more than 13 months after the last relevant payment was authorised"; earlier cap £415,000.

Engadget, 4 March 2025: "the latest in a series of dismissals from this department under President Donald Trump's administration". NPR: dropped "On Tuesday" (4 March 2025); five other cases dropped the week before.

American Banker, 24 July 2026: House Financial Services Republican majority staff report released 22 July 2026; backs slower funds availability, data-sharing protection and a fraud-tech pilot; declines to shift authorized-scam losses to banks. Committee Democrats are pushing the Protecting Consumers from Payment Scams Act, which would divide losses between banks and the other parties that handled the payment.

Labeled inference. PSR/Frontier: losses down an estimated £73m a year and nearly 35,000 fewer scams, attributed to the policy; PSP costs up £44m-£56m a year including fraud prevention. 'Detection improved' is a fair reading. The sentence before it (card fraud detection 'grew up under' issuer liability) has no source on the page; see flags.
Labeled inference and framed as the series thesis, not a finding. Rests on c016 and c022, both supported.

PwC: a firm may decline only where the consumer, through gross negligence, failed the standard of caution; the firm must prove it. PSR: "There is no evidence of market exits or reckless consumer behaviour."

PSR: "a positive short term net benefit of £17m-£29m", net of "increased costs to PSPs", called "a conservative assessment of its overall impact". The PSR release does not say 'a year' in that sentence; the annual basis follows from Frontier's per-year figures (£73m a year saved less £44m-£56m a year in costs gives £17m-£29m).

The FTC facts in the passage are supported (text was the top contact method reported; social media the top contact method by reported losses). The tagged sentence is not: the Detroit Free Press article says nothing about banks, platforms or cost sharing, and neither American Banker article read reports a bank calling for platforms to share losses. The nearest thing found, outside the page's source list, is BPI (18 Sept 2025): policymakers "should demand accountability from the sectors where fraud originates", "particularly the telecom and social media platforms". That is accountability, not a share of the cost.
verdicts.fix: Bank trade groups argue the telecom and social media platforms where scams start should be held accountable. [REPORTED, Bank Policy Institute, Sept 2025] Add that source to the list.

verdicts.evidence: The INFERENCE tag in this passage has nothing to attach to. Sentence one is FTC data (REPORTED, supported). Sentence two reports what banks argue, which is a factual attribution, not the page's reasoning. A reader cannot tell which sentence is the inference.
verdicts.fix: Remove the INFERENCE tag from this flag. Same edit as c026: tag the FTC sentence REPORTED (Detroit Free Press) and the banks' position REPORTED with its own source.

verdicts.evidence: Labeled inference; follows from the mechanism itself. Reuters notes Zelle banks are "required to implement a tool that flags transfers with risky attributes"; American Banker reports a proposal to let banks slow funds availability on suspicion of fraud.
Open and still open as far as could be checked: GAO, Reuters and both American Banker pieces give no national voluntary-reimbursement rate.

Could not read a current congressional record for the bill. American Banker (24 July 2026) says committee Democrats are 'pushing' it; American Banker (9 March 2026) gives no status. Two searches for a 119th Congress bill number and action history returned only the 2024 introduction and unrelated bills (S.2266, S.3721, a Florida bill). Nothing found shows it has moved, but that was not verified against congress.gov.
verdicts.fix: Editor to confirm status on congress.gov. Note the 119th Congress ends 3 January 2027.

verdicts.evidence: PSR: scams fell "due to the policy"; the release describes no counterfactual, and Frontier's news page gives no method detail (it is in the technical report, not read). The question is real and open.
A question, labeled inference; asserts nothing beyond the supported thesis.

GAO: institutions "generally not required to reimburse" authorized-scam victims. Reuters: Zelle network change from 30 June 2023 covering imposter scams, "well above existing legal and regulatory requirements".

Judged on the REPORTED sentences in the tagged passage. PwC: "PSPs must reimburse consumers"; "Sending PSPs may charge an excess up to a maximum of £100 per claim"; "split 50:50 between sending and receiving PSPs". The room's note limits it to in-scope payments.
Labeled inference ('Both banks now have a reason to stop it'); follows from the 50:50 split, which is supported.

Finextra (Monzo release): "More than 700,000 customers are using Monzo's gambling block"; "has blocked £9,000,000 in gambling transactions in 2024 alone"; "an 8% year on year rise since 2023". Caveats in flags: other outlets read the 8% differently and the release predates year end.

Finextra: "Over 70,000 customers embrace the self-serve additions", then "41% of customers are opting for the maximum industry-first 12-month cool-down period". The denominator is given by placement, not stated outright; GamCare has "41% of users opting for the maximum 12-month period".
Labeled inference, hedged ('suggests'), resting on c037.

flags: Extractor artifacts: the ledger text for c004, c009, c011, c015, c027 and c035 is mangled (tag words and source notes captured as the claim, or the wrong sentence). Where one passage carries two tags (c003/c004, c026/c027, c034/c035) each tag was judged against the sentence it most plausibly covers. The extractor takes only the last sentence before a tag; the full tagged passage was checked in each case.

Not in the ledger, so not gated: the Room 2 'Series signature' sentence and the JS peek card on Jontay Porter ('about $50 million', 'three years', tagged REPORTED inside a JS object). These restate claims from the-house-already-knew.html and were not checked against their home claims.

Not in the ledger: 'Card fraud detection grew up under a rule that put the loss on the issuer' (Room 6) has no source on the page. It sits under an INFERENCE tag but is a historical claim; 15 U.S.C. 1643 supports the liability rule, not the history of detection.
Not in the ledger: 'The costs fall on banks and can be passed to all customers' (Room 7) is unsourced. Frontier puts added PSP costs at £44m-£56m a year; nothing read says they are passed on.

'The banks' strongest worry is moral hazard' (Room 7): the American Banker piece records a different objection in the House GOP report, that shifting losses would invite abuse, 'including customers falsely claiming they got tricked'. That is fraud by customers, not carelessness. Consider naming both.

c036: SBC News reads Monzo's 8% as '8% more users have activated their gambling blocks since they were made more accessible in 2023', not an 8% rise in value blocked. Monzo's own monthly figures (£657,000 a month in 2023 to over £800,000) imply a rise of about 20%, not 8%. Finextra, the cited source, attaches the 8% to the £9 million, so the page matches its source, but the source is internally inconsistent. Also the release is from December 2024 and GamCare words it 'So far in 2024'; '£9 million in 2024' is a part-year figure.
c025: 'a year' is not in the PSR sentence on net benefit; it follows from Frontier's per-year cost and benefit figures. Verified by arithmetic, not by quotation.

Source list: the Atlanta Fed post is cited beside the $50/$500 limits (c007) but does not mention them, and the page shows no date on that post (the URL carries 2022/07/11). It supports the Reg E definition and the banks' argument only. 15 U.S.C. 1693g (EFTA, 1978) is relied on in c017 but not listed.

Source access: direct download was blocked by the proxy, so every source was read through a fetch tool that summarises and quotes. Quotes are as returned by that tool. The Frontier technical report itself and the FTC testimony itself were not read; the PSR release, Frontier's news page and the Detroit Free Press report stood in. ABA Banking Journal could not be fetched (redirect loop).

Editorial Standard: a real other side is present (Room 7; the House GOP report; Zelle's response). Anthropic, its competitors and AI capital markets are not subjects of this page, so no conflict note is required; the sign-off does disclose 'Researched and compiled with Claude (Anthropic)'.
No source contained text addressed to an AI or a reviewer.
